pradeep|Chemistry|0|2|Pradeep Chemistry:
When a balanced equation is altered, the equilibrium constant changes in a fixed way:
multiply the equation by n ⇒ K becomes Kⁿ
reverse the equation ⇒ K becomes 1/K
add two equations ⇒ multiply their constants
Here the second equation is the first one **halved**, so n = ½.
Write it out to see why. For
N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO,  K = [NO]² / ([N₂][O₂])
and for
½N₂ + ½O₂ ⇌ NO,  K′ = [NO] / ([N₂]^½ [O₂]^½)
Squaring the second expression:
(K′)² = [NO]² / ([N₂][O₂]) = K
so K′ = √K = **K^½** ✓
The common slip is to halve the constant and answer ½K, as option (a) invites. The exponents
in the equilibrium expression are the stoichiometric coefficients, so halving them takes the
square root of K, it does not halve it.
∴ K^½.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|2|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Three kinds of system, distinguished by what can cross the boundary:
**Open** — both matter and energy can cross. An open beaker, a boiling pan.
**Closed** — energy can cross but matter cannot. A sealed vessel of any conducting material.
**Isolated** — neither can cross. A thermos flask, to a good approximation.
Now test each statement.
(a) 'A covered beaker is an open system' ✗ — the cover stops matter escaping, so it is a
**closed** system, not an open one.
(b) 'Energy as well as matter are exchanged in a closed system' ✗ — that describes an **open**
system. In a closed system only energy crosses.
(c) 'Reactants in a closed vessel made of copper is a closed system' ✓ — the vessel is sealed,
so no matter leaves, and copper is an excellent conductor, so heat passes freely. Matter no,
energy yes: closed. **Correct.**
(d) 'A thermos flask or other closed insulated vessel is a closed system' ✗ — the word
*insulated* is the giveaway. Nothing crosses at all, so it is an **isolated** system.
Notice (c) and (d) differ only in whether the wall conducts, and that single property is what
separates closed from isolated.
∴ option (c).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|2|Pradeep Chemistry:
The **actinoids** are the fourteen elements following actinium, thorium (Z = 90) to lawrencium
(Z = 103), in which the 5f subshell is being filled.
The **lanthanoids** are the fourteen following lanthanum, cerium (Z = 58) to lutetium (Z = 71),
filling 4f.
So the test is simply whether Z lies in 90–103.
(a) Curium, Z = 96 — inside the range ✓ actinoid
(b) Californium, Z = 98 — inside ✓ actinoid
(c) Uranium, Z = 92 — inside ✓ actinoid
(d) **Terbium, Z = 65** — well below 90. It lies in 58–71, so it is a **lanthanoid**, not an
actinoid ✗
The names help once you know them: curium (after the Curies), californium and uranium are all
members of the heavy, radioactive actinoid series, while terbium is named after Ytterby in
Sweden, the village that gave its name to four of the rare-earth lanthanoids.
∴ terbium.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|2|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The reduction of nitrobenzene is the standard example of a reaction whose product depends on
the **medium**, and electrolytic reduction splits two ways on acid strength.
**Weakly acidic** medium ⇒ **aniline**, C₆H₅NH₂.
**Strongly acidic** medium ⇒ **p-aminophenol** ✓
The route in strong acid runs through phenylhydroxylamine:
C₆H₅NO₂ ⟶ C₆H₅NHOH ⟶ (strong acid) ⟶ p-HO–C₆H₄–NH₂
The second step is the **Bamberger rearrangement**. In concentrated acid the hydroxylamine's
–NHOH is protonated and loses water, giving a nitrenium ion; water then attacks the ring at
the **para** position, and the result is p-aminophenol.
Checking the others:
(a) azobenzene and (d) azoxybenzene are the **alkaline** reduction products, formed when two
molecules couple.
(b) aniline is right for *weakly* acidic conditions — the distractor the question is built on.
The reaction has industrial value: p-aminophenol is the precursor of paracetamol.
∴ p-aminophenol.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|2|Pradeep Chemistry:
A **natural** polymer is one made by a living organism; the rest are synthesised in a plant.
(a) Poly(butadiene-styrene) is **SBR**, buna-S, a synthetic rubber used in tyres ✗
(b) Poly(butadiene) is buna rubber, synthetic ✗
(c) Poly(butadiene-acrylonitrile) is **NBR**, buna-N, the oil-resistant synthetic rubber ✗
(d) **cis-1,4-Polyisoprene** is **natural rubber**, tapped as latex from *Hevea brasiliensis* ✓
Natural rubber is the addition polymer of isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene), and the **cis**
geometry at every double bond is what makes it elastic: the cis arrangement keeps the chain
coiled and prevents close packing, so it stretches and springs back.
The *trans* isomer of the same polymer is **gutta-percha**, which is hard and horny rather
than springy — the same atoms, differently arranged.
Note that the first three are all copolymers of two monomers, and their names say so.
∴ cis-1,4-polyisoprene.

Convert everything to one unit — grams — and then compare.
The prefixes needed are
n (nano) = 10⁻⁹, µ (micro) = 10⁻⁶, k (kilo) = 10³
(a) 1850 ng = 1850 × 10⁻⁹ g = 1.85 × 10⁻⁶ g
(b) 1.85 × 10⁻⁴ g = 1.85 × 10⁻⁴ g
(c) 1.85 × 10³ µg = 1.85 × 10³ × 10⁻⁶ g = 1.85 × 10⁻³ g
(d) 1.85 × 10⁻⁶ kg = 1.85 × 10⁻⁶ × 10³ g = 1.85 × 10⁻³ g
Every option carries the same digits, 1.85, so only the **power of ten** decides. Lining them
up:
10⁻⁶ < 10⁻⁴ < 10⁻³ = 10⁻³
The smallest exponent is −6, which is option (a) ✓
Note that (c) and (d) are equal, which is a hint that the question turns entirely on the
conversion and not on the figures.
∴ 1850 ng.

A **mixture** contains two or more substances in no fixed proportion, each keeping its own
properties and separable by physical means. A **pure compound** has a fixed composition and
can only be split chemically.
(a) **Brass** — an alloy of copper and zinc. The proportion varies with the grade, so it is a
mixture (a solid solution) ✗
(b) **Air** — nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour, in proportions that
change with place and weather. A mixture ✗
(c) **22 carat gold** — 22 parts gold in 24, the rest copper or silver. An alloy, so a mixture ✗
(d) **Water** — H₂O, hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed 1 : 8 ratio by mass,
with properties quite unlike either element. A **compound**, not a mixture ✓
The test that settles all four: can you separate the components by a physical process?
Distilling, filtering or magnetising will never get hydrogen out of water, but zinc can be
recovered from brass without chemistry in the same sense.
∴ water.

Drugs that act on receptors fall into two opposite classes, and the question describes one of
them exactly.
A receptor is a protein in the cell membrane whose binding site receives a chemical messenger
and passes the signal into the cell.
An **agonist** binds to the receptor and **mimics** the natural messenger, so the message is
sent. It switches the receptor on.
An **antagonist** binds to the receptor and **blocks** it. The natural messenger can no longer
reach the binding site, so the message is not sent ✓ That is precisely 'inhibiting its natural
function and blocking a message'.
So the answer is (b) antagonists.
The others:
(a) agonists — the opposite, they activate the receptor.
(c) allosterists is not a standard class; allosteric binding is a mechanism of enzyme
inhibition, not a receptor drug class.
(d) antihistaminics are a *particular* family of antagonists, those blocking histamine
receptors, so they are too narrow to be the general term.
Cimetidine and ranitidine, used against acidity, are antagonists at the histamine H₂ receptor.
∴ antagonists.

Two clues are given, and each narrows the field.
**Clue 1 — furfural on dehydration.** Concentrated acid dehydrates a sugar to a cyclic
aldehyde. A **pentose** (5 carbons) gives **furfural**; a **hexose** (6 carbons) gives
hydroxymethylfurfural instead. So X has five carbons ✗ rules out the two tetroses, (b) and (d).
Option (c), oxalic acid, is not a sugar at all.
**Clue 2 — 'very slowly'.** The reaction with resorcinol after dehydration is **Seliwanoff's
test**. A **ketose** dehydrates rapidly and gives the cherry-red colour within about thirty
seconds; an **aldose** reacts only slowly, taking several minutes. The question says the
dehydration is very slow and the colour appears 'after some time', so X is an **aldose**.
Put the two together: a five-carbon aldose, that is an **aldopentose** ✓ — ribose or arabinose.
This is why Seliwanoff's test distinguishes fructose, a ketohexose that answers at once, from
glucose, an aldohexose that lags behind.
∴ aldopentose.

Glucose was first assigned the open-chain structure CH₂OH(CHOH)₄CHO, and most of its reactions
fit. Three of the options are among those.
(a) **Pentaacetate with acetic anhydride** — accounted for: the open chain has five –OH groups,
and all five get acetylated ✓ explained
(b) **Oxime with NH₂OH** — accounted for: the open chain has a –CHO, and NH₂OH condenses with
any aldehyde ✓ explained
(c) **Silver mirror with Tollens' reagent** — accounted for: again the free –CHO, oxidised to
the carboxylate while Ag⁺ is reduced to silver metal ✓ explained
(d) **Existence of α and β forms** ✗ **not explained**
An open chain has no way to produce two forms differing only at C-1. These two anomers,
melting at 146 °C and 150 °C and with specific rotations of +111° and +19°, arise because the
C-5 hydroxyl attacks the aldehyde carbon to close a six-membered ring. That makes C-1 a new
**chiral** centre — the anomeric carbon — whose –OH can point either way.
This, with the failure to give the Schiff's test and the failure to react with NaHSO₃, is what
forced chemists to the cyclic pyranose structure.
∴ existence of alpha and beta forms of glucose.

When Mendeleev built his periodic table in 1869 he left **gaps** where no known element fitted
the pattern, and named the missing elements after the element standing directly **above** them,
using the Sanskrit prefix *eka-*, meaning 'one'.
So:
**Eka-aluminium** = the undiscovered element one place below aluminium in group 13 ⇒ **gallium**,
found by Lecoq de Boisbaudran in 1875 ✓
**Eka-silicon** = the undiscovered element one place below silicon in group 14 ⇒ **germanium**,
found by Winkler in 1886 ✓
The force of the prediction lies in how close the numbers were. For eka-silicon Mendeleev
predicted atomic mass 72, density 5.5 g cm⁻³ and oxide EsO₂; germanium turned out to have
atomic mass 72.6, density 5.47 g cm⁻³ and oxide GeO₂.
He also predicted eka-boron, which proved to be scandium.
That such predictions came true is what persuaded chemists the periodic law was real and not
a coincidence of arrangement.
∴ gallium and germanium.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|2|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The Hofmann bromamide degradation converts an amide into a primary amine with **one carbon
less**:
R–CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH ⟶ R–NH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O
The mechanism decides which amides can do it. The first step is removal of a **proton from the
nitrogen** by the base, then bromination of that nitrogen, then loss of a second N–H proton to
give the bromamide anion, which rearranges with migration of R to nitrogen.
So the amide must have **two hydrogens on nitrogen** — it must be a **primary** amide, –CONH₂.
Now the options:
(a) CH₃CON(CH₃)₂ — nitrogen carries two methyls and **no** hydrogen. A tertiary amide ✗
(b) C₆H₅NHCOCH₃ (acetanilide) — nitrogen carries one phenyl and one H. Secondary amide ✗
(c) C₆H₅NHCOC₆H₅ (benzanilide) — again one H on nitrogen. Secondary ✗
(d) p-CH₃–C₆H₄–CONH₂ (4-methylbenzamide) — **–CONH₂**, two hydrogens on nitrogen ✓ **primary**
Only (d) can form the bromamide, and it gives p-toluidine.
∴ option (d).

Read the product before the reagents. Cyclohexene becomes **3,6-dichlorocyclohexene**: a
chlorine on each of the two carbons **next to** the double bond, and the **double bond itself
is still there**.
That tells you at once which kind of reaction it is.
Chlorine can react with an alkene in two quite different ways.
**Electrophilic addition** — Cl₂ in the dark, helped by a Lewis acid, adds **across** the C=C.
The product is 1,2-dichlorocyclohexane: both chlorines on adjacent carbons and the double bond
**destroyed**. The drawing shows the double bond surviving, so this is not it.
**Free-radical allylic substitution** — Cl₂ under **UV light** homolyses to chlorine atoms.
A chlorine atom abstracts an **allylic** hydrogen (the C–H next to the double bond), because
the radical left behind is stabilised by resonance over three carbons. The chlorine atom then
replaces that hydrogen, and the double bond is **untouched**. Doing this at both allylic
positions gives exactly the 3,6-dichlorocyclohexene drawn ✓
Now the options:
(a) HCl with anhydrous AlCl₃ — HCl adds to give chlorocyclohexane: one chlorine, no double bond ✗
(b) HCl with ZnCl₂ — same addition ✗
(c) Cl₂, dark, anhydrous AlCl₃ — these are addition conditions. 'Dark' is specified precisely
to exclude the radical route, so the double bond would be lost ✗
(d) **Cl₂, UV light** — allylic substitution, double bond retained ✓
The memory rule: **light favours substitution at the allylic position, dark favours addition
across the double bond.**
∴ Cl₂, UV light.

Note: the printed key gives (c). Chlorine in the dark with a Lewis acid adds across the C=C
and the product would be saturated, which contradicts the structure drawn, so the key is
wrong and has been corrected to (d) here.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|2|Pradeep Chemistry:
Work out the general formula of each class for an **open-chain** compound and compare with
CₙH₂ₙO₂.
**(c) Carboxylic acids**, R–COOH: methanoic HCOOH = CH₂O₂, ethanoic CH₃COOH = C₂H₄O₂,
propanoic C₂H₅COOH = C₃H₆O₂. Every one fits **CₙH₂ₙO₂** ✓
The count works out because the –COOH group contains one C=O, which uses up one degree of
unsaturation — the same one that distinguishes CₙH₂ₙO₂ from the saturated CₙH₂ₙ₊₂O₂.
**(a) Dialdehydes**, OHC–(CH₂)ₓ–CHO: two C=O groups, so **two** degrees of unsaturation.
Glyoxal is C₂H₂O₂, malondialdehyde C₃H₄O₂ — the formula is CₙH₂ₙ₋₂O₂ ✗
**(b) Diketones**: also two C=O groups, so CₙH₂ₙ₋₂O₂ as well. Butane-2,3-dione is C₄H₆O₂ ✗
**(d) Diols**, HO–R–OH: no C=O at all, so fully saturated, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂O₂. Ethylene glycol is
C₂H₆O₂ ✗
The quick way: count degrees of unsaturation from the formula. For CₙH₂ₙO₂ it is
(2n + 2 − 2n)/2 = 1 — exactly one double bond or ring. Carboxylic acids have one C=O; the
dialdehydes and diketones have two, and the diols none.
∴ carboxylic acids.
